title: A Triple-Operator Decomposition of a Map from Causal to Correlational Brain Connectivity at Rest: Intrinsic Dynamics, Temporal Coloring, and Spatial Covariance
content: Correlational brain connectivity, roughly speaking, tells us how the activity from different brain regions covary. Causal brain connectivity, on the other hand, describes how different brain regions causally influence each other. Both types of brain connectivity at rest are commonly used for psychiatric classification in research settings, which is an important goal in computational psychiatry. Spectral dynamic causal modeling (DCM) is a widely used framework for inferring causal brain connectivity from resting state functional magnetic resonance imaging data. Crucially, spectral DCM entiles a deterministic map from causal to correlational brain connectivity, which can be expressed as a matrix-valued complex integral in the frequency domain. In the current study, we solve this matrix-valued integral and derive an analytic formula linking causal and correlational (more precisely covariance) patterns of brain connectivity. We show that this formula satisfies a Lyapunov equation with causal connectivity-dependent forcing, which is also the symmetrized zero-lag state--noise cross-covariance. Finally, we show that the steady-state covariance can be decomposed into three multiplicative factors (or operators) that have distinct roles, namely intrinsic neuronal dynamics (mean reversion), connectivity-dependent temporal coloring (scale-free), and a spatial covariance operator. Together, these results turn the deterministic relationship between causal and correlational brain connectivity in the frequency domain into a transparent algebraic formula that explains how intrinsic neuronal dynamics and the temporal and spatial characteristics of noise fluctuation jointly shape the correlational patterns of brain activity at rest.
